Option B is correct because passing environment-specific configuration into the stack through constructor props lets the same CDK code produce different, environment-appropriate resource configurations without duplicating the entire stack definition. Option C is incorrect because fully duplicating code for each environment increases maintenance burden and the risk of the environments drifting out of sync, compared to a single parameterized app. Option D is incorrect because manually editing code before each deployment is error-prone and defeats the purpose of a single, parameterized, reusable CDK app. Passing environment-specific configuration through stack props is the standard CDK pattern for a single codebase supporting multiple, differently configured environments.

questions.question: A team's CodePipeline includes a CodeBuild-based test stage that must have access to a private test database inside a VPC, but the CodeBuild project currently runs without VPC connectivity and cannot reach the database, causing tests to fail with connection timeouts. What must the developer configure to fix this?
options: Configure the CodeBuild project's VPC settings (VPC ID, subnets, and a security group) so build containers launch with network access to the private test database, and ensure the associated security group allows the necessary inbound access to the database
Enable CodeBuild's build badge feature
Increase the CodeBuild project's compute type to a larger instance size
Add a manual approval action before the test stage
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because CodeBuild projects can be optionally configured to run inside a specified VPC, subnets, and security group, which is required for build containers to reach resources, like a database, that are not publicly accessible. Option B is incorrect because the build badge only controls whether a status badge image is generated; it has no effect on network connectivity. Option C is incorrect because a larger compute type addresses CPU or memory constraints, not network connectivity to a private VPC resource. Option D is incorrect because a manual approval pauses the pipeline for human input; it does not provide the network path CodeBuild needs to reach the database. CodeBuild projects need explicit VPC configuration to reach resources inside a private VPC, since they do not have VPC connectivity by default.

questions.question: A developer wants a CloudFormation template to output the URL of a newly created API Gateway deployment stage, so that other stacks (or the developer) can easily retrieve it after stack creation without searching the console. Which template section should be used?
options: The Transform section
The Outputs section, referencing the API Gateway resource's generated invoke URL
The Parameters section
The Mappings section
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because the Transform section specifies macros (such as the SAM transform) applied to the template; it is unrelated to exposing an output value after deployment. Option B is correct because Outputs expose specific values from a stack after creation or update, which other stacks can import via cross-stack references or which a developer can view directly in the console or via the DescribeStacks API. Option C is incorrect because parameters are inputs provided when creating or updating a stack; they are not used to expose values generated during stack creation, like the resulting API URL. Option D is incorrect because mappings define static lookup tables for use elsewhere in the template; they do not expose values generated during deployment. Outputs are the CloudFormation section specifically for exposing generated values, such as a deployed API's invoke URL, after stack operations complete.

questions.question: A developer maintains a CDK app and wants to confirm, as part of CI, that a proposed change does not accidentally remove the DeletionPolicy or UpdateReplacePolicy protection that was intentionally set on a production database construct, protecting it from accidental deletion or replacement. Which TWO practices help guard against this in the CI pipeline? (Select TWO)
options: Rely on the AWS root user's MFA setting to catch this
Enable S3 versioning on the CDK app's source bucket
Increase the database instance's storage size
Use a CDK Aspect that validates the resource still has the expected RemovalPolicy set on affected constructs before allowing synthesis to succeed
Run cdk diff in the pipeline and fail the build if the review shows the protected resource would be replaced or removed
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because root user MFA protects account-level sign-in security and has no relationship to a specific CDK resource's removal policy. Option B is incorrect because source bucket versioning protects historical copies of files in that bucket; it does not validate the semantics of the CDK code's removal policy at build time. Option C is incorrect because storage size is unrelated to whether a removal or replacement policy has been accidentally changed. Option D is correct because a custom Aspect can programmatically inspect the construct tree and fail the build if a specific protected resource's RemovalPolicy has been removed or weakened. Option E is correct because diff output makes an unintended replacement or removal of the protected resource visible before it is applied, letting the pipeline stop the change automatically. Automated diff review and custom Aspects that assert specific protective settings remain in place are practical CI safeguards against accidental removal of resource protections.

questions.question: A developer wants CodeDeploy to deploy a new Lambda function version gradually, shifting 10% of traffic every 10 minutes over an hour, using a predefined configuration rather than a fully custom one. Which type of CodeDeploy deployment configuration fits this?
options: A Blue/Green deployment configuration with no traffic shifting settings
A predefined Canary deployment configuration such as Canary10Percent5Minutes
A predefined Linear deployment configuration for Lambda, such as Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes
An All-at-once deployment configuration
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because Lambda traffic shifting through CodeDeploy uses canary or linear configurations; a generic unconfigured blue/green setting does not define the specific gradual percentage-based rollout described. Option B is incorrect because canary configurations shift a single percentage of traffic and then, after a wait, shift the rest all at once, rather than continuing in equal linear increments over the whole hour. Option C is correct because Linear deployment configurations shift traffic in equal increments at a fixed interval, and the named predefined configurations directly match common patterns like 10% every 10 minutes. Option D is incorrect because all-at-once shifts 100% of traffic immediately, which does not match a gradual, incremental rollout requirement. Predefined Linear deployment configurations for Lambda match steady, incremental percentage-based traffic shifting over a defined total duration.

questions.question: A team's CloudFormation template uses a custom resource backed by a Lambda function to perform a one-time data migration whenever the stack is created or updated. During a recent update, the custom resource's Lambda function timed out before sending a response back to CloudFormation, causing the entire stack update to hang for the maximum wait period before failing. What should the developer change to make future custom resource failures fail fast instead of hanging?
options: Ensure the custom resource's Lambda function always sends a SUCCESS or FAILED response to the pre-signed S3 response URL, even on error, ideally wrapped so that timeouts or exceptions still trigger a FAILED response before the function's own execution ends
Switch the custom resource's service token to point directly at an SNS topic instead of Lambda
Add a DependsOn attribute from the custom resource to an unrelated S3 bucket
Increase the custom resource Lambda function's memory allocation
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because CloudFormation waits for an explicit response object to be sent back via the presigned URL, and if the function fails or times out without sending one, CloudFormation has no choice but to wait out its own timeout; explicitly catching errors and sending a FAILED response allows the stack operation to fail fast instead. Option B is incorrect because using SNS as the service token still requires some subscriber to eventually send the required response back to CloudFormation; simply switching the token type does not address the missing response handling. Option C is incorrect because DependsOn only affects resource ordering and does not address the missing response acknowledgment to CloudFormation. Option D is incorrect because more memory may reduce execution time for some workloads but does not guarantee a response is sent if the function still fails or times out without proper error handling. Custom resources must reliably send a response (success or failure) back to CloudFormation; without proper error handling, an unhandled timeout leaves CloudFormation waiting out its own operation timeout instead of failing fast.

questions.question: A developer is comparing CodeDeploy deployment types for an EC2/On-Premises compute platform. Which TWO statements correctly describe the difference between in-place and blue/green deployments? (Select TWO)
options: In-place deployments always require a completely separate Auto Scaling group from the original one

Blue/green deployments provision a new set of instances with the new revision and shift traffic to them only after they pass health checks, leaving the original instances unchanged until traffic is shifted
Blue/green deployments are only available for Lambda compute platforms, not EC2/On-Premises
Blue/green deployments cannot use an Elastic Load Balancer to manage traffic shifting
In-place deployments stop the application on each existing instance, install the new revision, and restart it, so some capacity is temporarily reduced during the deployment
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because in-place deployments update the existing instances directly and do not require provisioning a separate Auto Scaling group. Option B is correct because blue/green deployments avoid touching the original fleet until the new fleet is verified healthy, and traffic shifts only after that verification, unlike in-place updates. Option C is incorrect because blue/green deployments are available for EC2/On-Premises deployments as well as Lambda and ECS, not exclusively for Lambda. Option D is incorrect because blue/green deployments commonly rely on a load balancer to redirect traffic from the original environment to the replacement environment. Option E is correct because in-place deployment updates instances directly, meaning those instances are briefly unavailable to serve traffic while the new revision is installed and started. In-place deployments update existing instances directly (temporarily reducing capacity), while blue/green deployments stand up a new, verified fleet before shifting traffic.

questions.question: A developer notices that a Lambda function's CloudWatch metrics show a growing number of Throttles even though the function's own reserved concurrency has not been reached. What is a likely explanation the developer should check?
options: Throttles always indicate a bug in the function's code
The account-level (or another function-specific) concurrency limit may be constraining total concurrent executions across the account, separate from this function's own reserved concurrency setting
Throttles indicate the function's deployment package exceeds the size limit
Throttles only occur when a function's timeout is set too low
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because throttling reflects a concurrency capacity constraint, not necessarily a defect in the function's own logic. Option B is correct because Lambda enforces an account-wide concurrency limit in addition to any per-function reserved concurrency, so throttling can occur due to account-level exhaustion even when a specific function's own reserved concurrency has headroom. Option C is incorrect because package size issues cause deployment failures, not runtime throttling of invocations. Option D is incorrect because timeout duration is unrelated to whether an invocation is throttled due to concurrency limits. Account-level concurrency limits can throttle a function even when its own reserved concurrency setting has not been reached.

questions.question: A team observes that a Step Functions Standard state machine execution appears stuck in a RUNNING state far longer than expected, with the current state being a Task that invokes a Lambda function using the .waitForTaskToken pattern. CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function that should eventually call SendTaskSuccess show no recent invocations. What is the most likely explanation, and how should the team confirm it?
options: Step Functions executions automatically time out and fail after 5 minutes regardless of configuration
The state machine's IAM role lacks permission to invoke the Lambda function, causing it to hang silently

The external process responsible for calling SendTaskSuccess (or SendTaskFailure) with the correct task token never received or processed the token, so the execution is legitimately waiting; the team should check the execution's event history for the token and confirm whether the downstream system that should call back actually received it
CloudWatch Logs retention has expired for the relevant log group, making the execution appear stuck
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because Standard workflow executions can run for up to a year, and callback tasks specifically can wait much longer than 5 minutes if configured to do so. Option B is incorrect because a missing invoke permission would typically produce an explicit error in the execution's event history rather than an indefinitely running, silently waiting state. Option C is correct because the .waitForTaskToken pattern pauses the execution indefinitely (up to the configured timeout) until an external caller returns the token via SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure, so a stuck execution is expected behavior if that external callback never actually happens, and the event history reveals whether the token was issued and to whom. Option D is incorrect because log retention affects only how long log data is stored; it has no effect on the actual running state of a Step Functions execution. Callback pattern tasks can legitimately remain in a waiting state for a long time; checking the execution history for the issued token and confirming the external system received and processed it is the correct troubleshooting step.

questions.question: An API Gateway REST API integrated with a Lambda function using proxy integration intermittently returns HTTP 500 errors with the message 'Internal server error', and CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function show no corresponding invocation at all for the failed requests. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: The Lambda function's code has an unhandled exception that CloudWatch fails to log

The failures are occurring at the API Gateway layer itself, before or without successfully invoking Lambda, such as a Lambda invocation permission issue, a throttling event at the integration level, or an API Gateway-side error, rather than an error inside the function's code
The function's memory allocation is too low to log properly
API Gateway caching is serving a stale 500 error from cache
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because an unhandled exception inside a function that was actually invoked would still generate a log stream entry and a REPORT line; the absence of any invocation log points elsewhere. Option B is correct because if Lambda's own logs show no invocation for the failed requests, the failure is happening before the function actually runs, pointing to an API Gateway-to-Lambda integration issue (permissions, throttling, or a gateway-side problem) rather than application code. Option C is incorrect because memory allocation affects performance and execution characteristics, not whether invocation and error logs are written to CloudWatch. Option D is incorrect because caching a 500 error response would require it to have been cached from a specific prior response, and does not primarily explain a consistent pattern of missing corresponding Lambda logs across the errors. Missing Lambda invocation logs for failed requests points to a failure at the API Gateway-Lambda integration boundary, not inside the function's own code.

questions.question: A developer wants to compare the average latency of an API Gateway endpoint before and after a recent deployment, using a specific time range for each period. Which AWS tool is best suited for this comparison?
options: AWS Config timeline for the API Gateway resource
Amazon CloudWatch metrics (Latency or IntegrationLatency) graphed over the two relevant time ranges, optionally using metric math to compare periods
AWS X-Ray service map alone, without checking metrics
VPC Flow Logs for the API Gateway's network interfaces
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because Config tracks configuration changes to the resource over time, not runtime latency performance metrics. Option B is correct because API Gateway automatically publishes latency metrics to CloudWatch, which can be graphed and compared across any two time ranges to evaluate the effect of a deployment. Option C is incorrect because the X-Ray service map visualizes the architecture and relationships between components; comparing average latency over specific time periods is better done with CloudWatch metrics. Option D is incorrect because API Gateway is a managed service without customer-visible network interfaces to inspect via VPC Flow Logs in this way, and flow logs would not measure API-level latency in any case. CloudWatch metrics are the direct, built-in source for API Gateway latency data across any chosen time ranges for before/after comparison.

questions.question: A developer notices that a DynamoDB table's consumed write capacity spikes dramatically higher than expected whenever a particular batch job runs, even though the number of logical item updates performed by the job has not changed. Investigation shows the job recently began updating a Global Secondary Index's projected attributes on every write. What most directly explains the increased consumed capacity, and what should the developer check?
options: DynamoDB doubles consumed write capacity automatically whenever more than one GSI exists on a table, regardless of which attributes are touched
The batch job must be using BatchWriteItem, which always costs twice as much as individual PutItem calls
Provisioned throughput automatically increases capacity consumption reporting whenever DynamoDB Streams is enabled

Updates to attributes projected into a GSI also consume write capacity on that GSI in addition to the base table, so a change that newly touches a GSI's projected attributes on every write increases total consumed write capacity; the developer should review the GSI's projection type and consider projecting fewer attributes if not all are needed
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because GSIs only consume additional write capacity when a write actually changes an attribute that is projected into that specific index, not simply because multiple GSIs exist. Option B is incorrect because BatchWriteItem does not inherently cost more per item than individual PutItem calls; the described capacity increase is explained by the GSI projection change, not by the choice of batch versus individual API calls. Option C is incorrect because enabling Streams does not consume additional read or write capacity units and does not explain this consumption pattern. Option D is correct because every write that changes an attribute projected into a GSI results in a corresponding write to that index, so if the job's updates now touch a broader or newly projected set of attributes, this adds GSI write capacity consumption on top of the base table write, which the developer can reduce by projecting only necessary attributes. Writes affecting GSI-projected attributes consume additional write capacity on the index itself; reviewing and minimizing GSI projections is a direct way to control this cost.

questions.question: A developer wants to quickly determine whether a Lambda function's recent elevated error rate correlates with a specific deployment (a specific published version), to decide whether to roll back. Which approach provides this correlation most directly?
options: Check the function's IAM role's last-modified timestamp
Graph the Errors metric filtered or dimensioned by function version/alias in CloudWatch, aligned against the known deployment timestamps
Check the S3 bucket's versioning history for the deployment package
Review the function's reserved concurrency history
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because the role's last-modified timestamp reflects permission changes, not error rates tied to a specific code version. Option B is correct because filtering or dimensioning the Errors metric by version lets the developer directly see whether the error rate increase began coinciding with a specific version's rollout, rather than inferring it indirectly. Option C is incorrect because S3 object versioning tracks storage-level object history and does not directly present function error-rate metrics correlated to a version. Option D is incorrect because reserved concurrency is a capacity setting and does not by itself indicate whether errors correlate with a specific code version. Dimensioning CloudWatch metrics by function version/alias directly shows whether an error spike correlates with a specific deployment.

questions.question: A microservice calling another microservice inside the same VPC via an internal Application Load Balancer starts seeing a sharp increase in connection reset errors during peak traffic, while the target microservice's own CPU and memory remain low. The target's ALB target group health checks show all targets passing. What should the developer investigate next?
options: The VPC's DHCP option set must be misconfigured

Whether the target microservice's application-level connection or thread pool limits (for example, a web server's max concurrent connections setting) are being exceeded, causing it to actively reset excess connections even though system-level CPU and memory remain low
The ALB's idle timeout must be decreased to prevent connection resets
The target group's health check interval must be increased to catch failures faster
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because DHCP option sets affect DNS and domain name resolution behavior for instances, and are not a typical cause of connection resets tied to application-level connection limits under load. Option B is correct because an application can be configured with connection or thread limits well below what its underlying compute resources could otherwise support, so it can start resetting connections under load due to hitting an application-level cap, independent of CPU/memory utilization or ALB health check status. Option C is incorrect because decreasing the idle timeout would cause the load balancer to close connections sooner, which does not address a target actively resetting connections due to its own internal limits, and could make timeout-related issues worse. Option D is incorrect because health checks in this scenario show all targets passing, so an interval change would not affect why healthy-appearing targets are resetting connections under load. When infrastructure-level metrics look healthy but connections are still being reset under load, application-level connection or thread pool limits are a common, often-overlooked cause to investigate.

questions.question: A developer wants to identify which specific downstream AWS API calls made by a Lambda function are the slowest, across many different invocations, to prioritize optimization efforts. Which X-Ray feature provides this aggregated view rather than looking at one trace at a time?
options: The Lambda function's REPORT log lines from a single invocation
The X-Ray service map and the associated aggregated trace analytics, which summarize latency statistics per downstream node across many traces
AWS Config aggregated compliance view
CloudWatch composite alarms
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because a single invocation's REPORT line only shows aggregate duration for that one invocation, not a breakdown of which specific downstream call was slow across many invocations. Option B is correct because the service map, combined with the console's trace summary and analytics views, aggregates latency data across many traces per downstream call, showing which specific calls are consistently slow rather than requiring inspection of individual traces one at a time. Option C is incorrect because Config's aggregated view reports on resource configuration compliance, not application-level latency statistics for downstream calls. Option D is incorrect because composite alarms combine the state of several existing alarms into one; they do not provide a per-downstream-call latency breakdown across many traces. X-Ray's service map and trace analytics aggregate data across many traces, directly surfacing which downstream calls are consistently slow, unlike inspecting single traces individually.

questions.question: A developer notices that after switching a Lambda function's runtime from Node.js 16 to Node.js 20, cold start duration increased noticeably, and the function's memory usage also appears higher in CloudWatch metrics than before the runtime change, even though no application code was modified. What is a reasonable first troubleshooting step, given that the code itself did not change?
options: Compare the deployment package size and dependency versions resolved for the new runtime, since some dependencies may have pulled in different (larger) native binaries or transitive dependencies under the new runtime's package resolution, increasing both cold start time and memory footprint
Increase the function's timeout value to compensate
Assume the new runtime is broken and immediately roll back without further investigation
Assume this is unrelated to the runtime change since the application code is unchanged, and look for an unrelated infrastructure issue
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because runtime version changes can affect dependency resolution, potentially pulling in different package versions or native binaries, which can increase deployment package size and memory footprint even without any application code changes, so comparing packages before and after the runtime switch is a reasonable first diagnostic step. Option B is incorrect because increasing timeout does not address or explain the underlying increase in cold start duration and memory usage. Option C is incorrect because rolling back without investigation forgoes the chance to understand a root cause that might recur or that could be fixed with a smaller change than a full rollback. Option D is incorrect because runtime changes can affect behavior even without application code changes, due to differences in dependency resolution, the runtime's own initialization behavior, or default settings, so dismissing the runtime change as unrelated skips the most direct explanation. A runtime version change can alter dependency resolution and initialization behavior even without code changes, making a before/after comparison of the deployment package a sensible first troubleshooting step.

questions.question: A developer wants to be alerted automatically if a Lambda function's error rate exceeds 5% over any 5-minute period, rather than manually checking dashboards. Which AWS capability should be configured?
options: A CloudWatch alarm using a metric math expression that computes Errors divided by Invocations over a 5-minute period, with a threshold of 0.05
A CloudTrail Insights rule on the function's ARN
An AWS Config rule checking the function's configuration every 24 hours
An S3 event notification on the function's deployment bucket
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because CloudWatch alarms support metric math expressions, allowing a derived metric like error rate (errors divided by invocations) to be evaluated against a threshold and trigger a notification automatically. Option B is incorrect because CloudTrail Insights identifies unusual API call volume patterns, not application-level error rates derived from custom metric math. Option C is incorrect because Config rules evaluate configuration state, not runtime error-rate metrics computed over rolling time windows. Option D is incorrect because S3 event notifications react to object-level events in a bucket and have no relationship to a function's runtime error rate. CloudWatch alarms with metric math expressions are the standard way to compute and alert on a derived metric like error rate over a specific time window.

questions.question: A developer is debugging why a Lambda function subscribed to a Kinesis Data Stream is falling behind (IteratorAge metric is growing) even though the function's own duration per invocation is short and concurrency looks healthy. Which TWO factors could explain a growing IteratorAge in this scenario? (Select TWO)
options: The stream has more shards than the event source mapping's configured parallelization factor can keep up with given the incoming record volume per shard
A small number of records are repeatedly failing and being retried without bisecting or a configured maximum retry limit, blocking progress on their shard
Enhanced fan-out was enabled on a different, unrelated consumer
The function's reserved concurrency was set higher than needed
The stream's retention period was increased
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because if incoming throughput per shard exceeds what the configured number of parallel consumers per shard can process in time, records back up and the iterator falls further behind. Option B is correct because a stuck batch that keeps retrying without ever succeeding or being given up on can block the consumer from advancing on that shard, causing the iterator age to keep growing. Option C is incorrect because fan-out configured for a separate consumer does not affect this function's own processing rate against the stream. Option D is incorrect because having more reserved concurrency than needed does not cause a consumer to fall behind; insufficient concurrency or throughput would be the concern, not excess. Option E is incorrect because increasing retention allows records to remain in the stream longer but does not itself cause the consumer to fall behind processing new records. Growing IteratorAge is typically explained by insufficient per-shard processing throughput or a stuck/repeatedly failing batch blocking progress on a shard.
